title: Mantra repetition
hookLine: repeating a sacred name or mantra, often on beads

cards: A string of wooden beads hangs on a hook by a kitchen door, one spot worn smooth. Early, before the kettle, a hand takes it down. A thumb pulls one bead toward the palm.
Lips move. A name is said, barely above a breath. Next bead.
Same name. No new words are added. Nothing is asked for.
The kettle boils and is ignored for a moment longer. Yesterday the mind was a lake, moving in the wind. Today, a way of giving it one place to move.

teach.h: A SACRED NAME, AGAIN AND AGAIN.
teach.b: That's japa: the repetition of a sacred name or a mantra, said aloud, whispered, or held silently. You met the mantra back on day one hundred two, a word carried on the breath.
Different Hindu communities repeat different names. Devotees of Shiva may repeat Om namah Shivaya; devotees of Rama, the name Ram.
It's often counted on a string of beads called a mala, so the hand keeps the count and the mind doesn't have to. And it turns up in yesterday's book.
In the Yoga Sutras, sutra one point twenty-seven says the word that expresses the Lord is the pranava, the sacred syllable Om.

The next sutra gives the practice in two parts: its repetition, japa, and dwelling on its meaning. Not sound alone, not meaning alone: the word, said again and again, with attention on what it points to.
From that, the following sutra says, comes turning inward, and the clearing of what stands in the way. The Bhagavad Gita goes further.

There Krishna names, kind by kind, what he is among things, and among the forms of sacrifice, he says, he is japa, the sacrifice of repetition. A sacrifice that needs no fire, no food, no money. Only breath and a name.
So japa isn't saying a word until it means nothing.

teach.h: ONE GROOVE, LIKE THE SMOOTH BEAD.
teach.b: In this picture the word is said so often that the mind, which moves all day, gets worn into one groove, like the smooth spot on the bead.

how: Hindus who practice japa repeat a mantra or a name of God such as Ram or Om namah Shivaya, often counting on a mala of beads, aloud, in a whisper, or silently.

o: a breathing count used to help you fall asleep
a prayer asking God for one particular favor
repeating a sacred name, often on prayer beads

p: a string of beads to keep count
Om, the word for the Lord

s: japa must always be said out loud
it can be said aloud, whispered, or held silently in the mind.
in the Yoga Sutras, japa comes paired with dwelling on the word's meaning
sutra 1.28: its repetition, and dwelling on its meaning. both halves together.
in the Gita, Krishna names japa among the forms of sacrifice
a sacrifice that needs no fire, no food and no money: only breath and a name.

games.q: you're repeating Om on your beads, and realize you've said it twenty times while planning lunch. by sutra 1.28, what's missing?
o: the meaning: attention on what the word points to.
games.why: the sutra asks for two things together: the repetition, and dwelling on its meaning. you kept the sound and dropped the meaning. so you just pick it back up.

practice: Choose one word and keep it: if you pray, a name from your own tradition, and if you don't, a plain word like peace, or here.

Say it softly or inside twenty-seven times, three rounds of nine on your fingers, letting a little of the meaning come with each one. When you lose count, don't start over in frustration; just go on from where you think you were.

wordCard.voice: Japa. The repetition of a sacred name or mantra, often counted on beads, aloud, whispered or silent, with attention on its meaning. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: japa. Next bead, same name, and the groove gets a little deeper. Until tomorrow.
